opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The Grand Illusion paper started from a simple question: we talk about these frameworks as if they're hardware-agnostic. You write your model in PyTorch, JAX, or TensorFlow, and in principle it should run anywhere. We wanted to test whether that's actually true.

What we found is that portability is much more of an illusion than people assume. When you move between hardware types, say from GPUs to TPUs or the other way around, a surprisingly large share of functions either fail outright or only partially work. Even when a function does run, it's often dramatically slower, sometimes by an order of magnitude or more. That slowdown makes it practically unusable for real research.

The pattern is telling. Each framework tends to work best on the hardware it grew up with. JAX and TensorFlow are deeply tuned for TPUs, and PyTorch is tuned for GPUs. Once you step outside that pairing, the experience degrades a lot. So the framework doesn't really free you from the hardware. It ties you more tightly to a particular hardware and software stack.

That matters for a few reasons.

**It shapes which ideas get explored.** This links back to my earlier work on the hardware lottery. Ideas succeed partly because they fit the available hardware and software, not purely on merit. If your idea needs an operation that's slow or broken on the hardware you have, you may drop it, not because it's a bad idea but because the tooling punished you for trying.

**It concentrates power.** If you have access to a particular kind of accelerator, you get a smooth experience. If you don't, you pay a large tax in engineering time and compute. That widens the gap between well-resourced labs and everyone else.

**It discourages hardware diversity.** If moving to new hardware means much of your stack breaks, there's a huge switching cost. New chips struggle to gain adoption even when they might be better suited to emerging workloads. The ecosystem reinforces itself.

So the bigger takeaway for me is that we need to treat portability as a first-class research and engineering goal, not an assumption. That means better benchmarking of functions across hardware, more investment in compilers and intermediate representations that genuinely abstract over devices, and honesty in the community that our tools aren't neutral. They quietly steer the direction of the field, and we should be aware of that if we want progress driven by ideas rather than by whichever hardware happens to be dominant.

r001.rationale: The response describes portability problems and switching costs, but does not say hardware lock-in is hard to assess because its constraints often become apparent only retrospectively.

r002.rationale: It says the frameworks are treated as hardware-agnostic, then explains that each is tuned for particular hardware and performance degrades outside that pairing.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes functions that fail or only partially work from functions that run but are so slow as to be practically unusable.

r004.rationale: It says JAX is deeply tuned for TPUs and that performance degrades outside its hardware pairing, which attributes GPU slowdowns to its TPU focus.

r005.rationale: The response does not discuss Transformers or explain how hardware specialization could make a shift to a fundamentally different architecture harder.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So the Grand Illusion paper was really about asking a very simple question that, surprisingly, nobody had rigorously tested: can you actually take a model written in one of the major frameworks and just move it across hardware? The implicit promise of these frameworks is portability. You write your JAX or PyTorch or TensorFlow code once, and in theory you should be able to run it on a GPU, a TPU, whatever accelerator you have. And what we found is that this promise is, in many cases, an illusion.

We took a set of functions and models and tried to run them across different device types, and a large fraction of them either failed outright, or they ran but with significant performance degradation, or in some cases they ran but produced different numerical results. And the failures were very asymmetric. PyTorch, for example, is quite reliable on GPUs but much less so on TPUs. JAX is the reverse, it's been co-developed with TPUs so it works well there, and then on GPUs you'd see a lot of functions that were either unsupported or much slower than you'd expect. TensorFlow sat somewhere in the middle, but it had its own set of gaps.

What I think this reveals about lock-in is that the lock-in isn't really happening at the level of the framework choice in isolation. It's happening at the intersection of framework and hardware. The software stack has become so entangled with specific hardware that your choice of framework is effectively a choice of hardware, and vice versa. And that's a kind of lock-in that's quite invisible, because on paper everything is open source and portable. Nobody is explicitly stopping you from running JAX on a GPU. It's just that the work of making those kernels fast and correct hasn't been done evenly, because the incentives of the organizations maintaining these frameworks are tied to particular hardware ecosystems.

This connects to the hardware lottery argument I've made before. The idea there was that research ideas win or lose partly based on whether they happen to fit the available hardware and software. And what the Grand Illusion results suggest is that this is getting narrower, not wider. We're converging on a small number of hardware-software pairings that are well optimized, and anything outside those pairings, whether that's a new accelerator or a new type of model architecture that needs different operations, faces a really steep hill. So if you're a researcher with an unconventional idea, or a company trying to introduce new hardware, the portability gap is a real barrier, and it compounds over time because the well-trodden paths keep getting more optimized while everything else stagnates.

The other thing I'd say is that this has implications for who gets to do research. If the only way to get reasonable performance is to be inside an ecosystem that has deep access to a particular hardware stack, that concentrates capability in a small number of organizations. So I think portability is not just an engineering nicety. It's actually a question about the diversity of ideas we get to explore as a field.

r001.rationale: The response calls lock-in invisible, but does not say its constraints are difficult to assess until they become apparent retrospectively.

r002.rationale: It says the frameworks’ promise of portability is often an illusion and that framework and hardware choices are entangled.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes functions that fail, functions that run with significant performance degradation, and functions that produce different numerical results.

r004.rationale: It says JAX was co-developed with TPUs and works well there, while on GPUs many functions are unsupported or much slower.

r005.rationale: It says unconventional architectures needing different operations face a steep hill, but does not connect that difficulty to hardware specialization for Transformers or a future shift away from them.

astra-6.text:
I think they reveal that hardware lock-in is also a software problem. We tend to think, “If I’m using a framework like JAX, TensorFlow, or PyTorch, it abstracts away the hardware, so I should be able to move my model.” But that abstraction doesn’t necessarily give you portability in practice—and particularly portability of performance.

There’s a difference between getting something to run on another accelerator and getting it to run efficiently. Your implementation depends on which operations are supported, how those operations are compiled, and where optimization effort has gone. So even if the model looks hardware-independent at one level, the software stack can tie it quite tightly to a particular platform.

That matters because the cost of switching isn’t just buying different hardware. It’s engineering time, reworking code, and potentially losing performance. A new hardware platform has to compete with that whole ecosystem, not just with another chip. And that can reinforce the incumbent’s advantage while making it harder to explore alternatives.

r001.rationale: The response describes switching costs and platform dependence, but does not say lock-in is difficult to assess or becomes apparent only retrospectively.

r002.rationale: It names JAX, TensorFlow, and PyTorch, then explains that their hardware abstraction does not ensure practical portability and that the software stack can tie implementations to a platform.

r003.rationale: It explicitly distinguishes getting a model to run on another accelerator from getting it to run efficiently.

r004.rationale: It does not attribute JAX GPU slowdowns to development with TPUs in mind.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss Transformer-specific hardware specialization or the difficulty of shifting to a fundamentally different architecture.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important distinction is between portability in principle and portability in practice. We often say, “Well, you can use JAX, TensorFlow, or PyTorch, so you have this abstraction layer between your model and the hardware.” But being able to run a model somewhere else doesn’t mean you can run it efficiently, or that moving it is straightforward.

The Grand Illusion findings point to how much of that abstraction depends on the underlying software stack: the compiler, the kernels, the libraries, and the optimizations for a particular device. So the lock-in isn’t just the chip. It’s the accumulated investment in making that whole stack work well together. Supporting the same framework doesn’t automatically give another hardware platform comparable performance.

And that matters for research, because the experiments we can afford to run influence the ideas we pursue. If an approach works well on the dominant hardware, it’s easier to explore and scale. So hardware lock-in can also narrow the space of ideas we investigate. That’s why I think meaningful portability has to include the cost and performance of moving, not simply whether the code executes.

r001.rationale: The response discusses lock-in and its effects but does not say its constraints are difficult to assess or become apparent only retrospectively.

r002.rationale: It explains that framework abstractions depend on the underlying device-specific software stack and optimizations, so framework support alone does not remove hardware dependence.

r003.rationale: It explicitly distinguishes being able to run a model elsewhere from running it efficiently or with comparable performance.

r004.rationale: It does not attribute JAX GPU slowdowns to development with TPUs in mind.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss Transformer specialization or how that could impede a shift to a fundamentally different architecture.
